headline: Forgotten old apples may return to Austrian stores

sources.title: Spar und Frutura testen Anbau alter Apfelsorten (Vienna.at)
Core values: the Austrian scheme bringing forgotten apple varieties back to life (The Guardian)
Major Supermarket Begins Wide-Scale Tests to Bring Heritage Apple Varieties to Market (Good News Network)

chunks.text: Apples that Austrians ate more than 100 years ago may soon return to stores. On October 14, 2026, one of Austria's biggest [[supermarket chains]] presented a [[test project]] with the country's largest fruit and vegetable [[supplier]]. They want to {{bring back}} forgotten apple [[varieties]]. Austria has about 2,000 kinds of apples, but stores sell only about ten. War, [[industrial farming]] and [[a taste for]] sweet fruit nearly {{wiped out}} many old types.

verbs.why: Many towns bring back old festivals in the summer. Some stores bring back popular snacks every fall. Two companies in Austria want to bring back forgotten apple varieties.

verbs.wrong: To change the taste of something
verbs.why: Hungry insects wipe out whole fields of corn in some years. A bad storm sometimes wipes out a town's power lines. War, industrial farming and a taste for sweet fruit nearly wiped out many old apple types.

chunks.text: A team at the chain that works to protect bees {{came up with}} the idea in 2023. The chain's [[deputy chair]] said the reason is not [[romantic]]. It is about [[biodiversity]], the variety of plant and animal life. Experts from a group that saves [[rare plants]] helped {{narrow the list down}} to two varieties from the 1800s. One may no longer grow anywhere [[in the wild]]. The supplier had to travel to a [[research center]] in northern Italy to {{track down}} its trees.

verbs.correct: To find something after a long search

chunks.text: The supplier {{put in}} about 2,150 trees. Three years later, they gave their first [[harvest]], roughly one metric ton of apples. The larger apple has a [[deep red]] color. The other is smaller and [[paler]]. A manager at the supplier said both remind people of the apples they ate {{growing up}}. The team wants to {{find out}} how well the apples {{hold up}} in [[storage]]. It will also test how well the trees fight disease.

verbs.correct: To plant something in the ground
verbs.why: Many families put in a vegetable garden every spring. Farmers put in new trees when old ones die. The supplier put in about 2,150 trees, and after three years they gave their first harvest.
Many children grow up with a pet in the house. Kids grow up fast in big families. A manager said both apples remind people of the apples they ate growing up.

verbs.correct: To learn a fact or the truth
verbs.why: Students find out their test scores on Friday. Most people find out the news on their phones. The team wants to find out how well the old apples last in storage.

verbs.correct: To stay good for a long time
verbs.why: Cheap shoes do not hold up in the rain. Good jeans hold up for years. The team wants to see how well the old apples hold up in storage.

chunks.text: Only a little of the first harvest will reach a store in Vienna. Most of the fruit will probably {{end up}} with the two companies. The old apples will cost a little more than others. Still, the deputy chair promised that everyone can [[afford]] them. Nobody knows yet whether they will {{catch on}} with shoppers. The same manager says farming mixes new ideas with knowledge {{passed down}} through [[generations]].

verbs.why: Lost phones often end up at the front desk. Old clothes sometimes end up in a store for used goods. Most of the first apples will probably end up with the two companies.
New dance moves catch on fast with teenagers. Some new foods never catch on in small towns. Nobody knows yet whether the old apples will catch on with shoppers.

mainIdea.s: A large Austrian store chain is testing two apple types that people grew long ago. The goal is more variety on shelves, but nobody knows yet if shoppers will want them.
mainIdea.why: The chain and a big supplier want to bring back forgotten apples. The first harvest is small, and it is not clear if the apples will catch on.

mainIdea.s: An Austrian supermarket wants old apple types mainly because they cost less to grow. Its leaders hope this will let them sell fruit at lower prices than other stores.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the project is about biodiversity, not saving money. The old apples will also cost a little more than other apples.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in Austria have created a new apple that stays fresh for a full year. Farmers plan to plant it widely because it needs far less water than older kinds.
mainIdea.why: This story is about testing very old apple types. Experts helped narrow the list down to two varieties from the 1800s.

tf.s: A supermarket chain wants to bring back forgotten apple varieties.
tf.why: The chain and Austria's largest fruit and vegetable supplier are testing old apple types.

tf.s: Only a few of Austria's many apple varieties are sold in stores.
tf.why: Austria has about 2,000 kinds, but only about ten are in stores. Many old types were nearly wiped out.

tf.s: The project started because the chain's leaders felt romantic about the past.
tf.why: The deputy chair said the reason is biodiversity, not romance. A team that works to protect bees came up with the idea.

tf.s: The team wants to find out how well the old apples hold up in storage.
tf.why: The team is checking how long the apples stay fresh. It will also test how well the trees fight disease.

tf.s: Most of the first harvest will be sold in stores across Austria.
tf.why: Only a small amount will reach one store in Vienna. Most of the fruit will probably end up with the two companies.

tf.s: It is still not clear whether the old apples will catch on with shoppers.
tf.why: Nobody knows yet how shoppers will feel about the apples, which will cost a little more than others.

lines.text: Did you hear that a big supermarket chain in Austria wants to {{bring back}} old apples?
Old apples? You mean apples that sat in a warehouse for months?
No, old kinds of apples. One of them is from about 1840.
Oh, so it's [[a blast from the past]].
Exactly. Austria has about 2,000 kinds of apples, but stores sell only about ten.
Wow. What happened to the rest?
War and big modern farms almost {{wiped out}} a lot of them.
So how did they even get the trees?
The fruit company had to travel all the way to Italy to {{track down}} one kind.
That's a lot of work for an apple. How do they taste?
A manager said they taste like the apples people ate {{growing up}}.
I love that. [[You can't beat]] a sweet, crunchy apple in the fall.
They still need to {{find out}} how well the apples {{hold up}} in storage, though.
Will they cost more than normal apples?
A little more. But the chain says everyone will be able to afford them.
Well, [[you get what you pay for]].
The big question is whether they'll {{catch on}} with shoppers.
I hope they do. [[Variety is the spice of life]], right?

ex: I try a new restaurant every month. Variety is the spice of life.
